grade.first_issue: In Case 3, the claim that an arithmetic progression tending to infinity must start to the right of the finite forbidden interval is false; it may begin to the left and skip the interval. Moreover, the previously defined y_0 is naturally a zero-defect point, in which case y_n=y_0+n c_1 is not its orbit. Thus the mixed zero/positive-defect case is not validly resolved.
grade.summary: The classification is correct, and the proof correctly verifies the candidates, proves g≥0, and essentially establishes equality of all positive values of g. However, the exclusion of simultaneous defect values 0 and c>0 contains a false inference and then asserts without proof that the two level sets must be complementary intervals. This unsupported central structural claim is load-bearing, so Rule E caps the score at 3; Rule B does not permit 4 because the missing compatibility argument is not reduced to an explicit equality.
strengths: Correctly verifies every f(x)=x+c with c≥0 using RMS–AM–GM.
Correctly obtains f(f(y))=2f(y)-y, invariance of g along forward orbits, and g≥0.
The orbit-comparison argument gives meaningful progress toward proving that any two positive values of g are equal.
The submitted final classification agrees with the true answer.

errors.description: In the mixed-defect case, y_n→∞ does not imply that y_0 lies to the right of the forbidden interval; an arithmetic progression can start to its left and avoid it. The displayed formula y_n=y_0+n c_1 is also inconsistent if y_0 is the zero-defect point chosen earlier.

The statement that S_0∪S_{c_1}=(0,∞) implies S_0=(0,b] and S_{c_1}=(b,∞) is false without first proving an ordering or interval property of the level sets. That missing structural step is essential to the final contradiction.
Even after proving separation by a threshold, the boundary could belong to S_{c_1} rather than S_0; the proof handles only one of these two endpoint cases.
